newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: EU trade perks not enough to help Yugo agriculture.
newsitem.headline: EU trade perks not enough to help Yugo agriculture.

text.p: Yugoslavia's ailing agriculture and food industries need much more than European Union trade preferences to meet export targets, the Belgrade-based Institute for Foreign Trade said on Thursday.

"Without some kind of logistical support, through instruments of agriculture and trade policy, EU trade preferences alone will not substantially help raise exports," institute economist Vojislav Stankovic told Reuters in an interview.
The EU in April granted trade privileges to Yugoslavia, relaxing restrictions on its exports to European markets.

The agriculture and food sectors, widely seen by policy makers as having the greatest potential to expand exports, are burdened by shortage of cash, high debts, outdated machinery and lack of subsidies.
"Nobody in the world exports without subsidies. For example, the degree of support in some countries goes up to an average 45 percent," Stankovic said.
Agriculture subsidies in Yugoslavia are now just 1-3 percent and are paid irregularly, with delays of up to nine months, Stankovic said.
Apart from loss of foreign markets, an influx of cheaper, heavily subsidised foreign agricultural and food products have narrowed the domestic market as well.
"This country needs some kind of supra-government administration that will control certain strategic products like tobacco and alcoholic drinks," said Stankovic.
The industry, which kept up production during the difficult years of sanctions, is neglected and will collapse unless the state helps, Stankovic said.
He said EU measures would provide no more than $60 million a year benefit to the sector.

According to the institute's latest report, January-April agriculture and food exports were worth $147.6 million, accounting for 21.8 percent of total commodity exports, but only 20.2 percent of the targetted $729 million in 1997.
Imports of food and agricultural goods in the same period stood at $197.5 million, or 14.8 percent of commodity imports.

Top imports included live cattle, beef, canned and processed meats, other canned foodstuffs, milk and milk products, cheese, eggs, wheat, maize, fresh and dried fruits, sugar, coffee, chocolates and non-alcoholic beverages.
The industry's exports to the EU in 1996 stood at $170.7 million, or a third of its total exports of some $535 million.
Exports to the EU in the first four months of this year were $37.7 million, or 22.2 percent of the total exports of $147.6 million.

"You can draw your own conclusions from these figures about official forecasts for agriculture exports this year, which go as high as $2 billion," Stankovic said. -- Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
